utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, everybody. Before we hear the witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to raise? Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have a short matter, but I think it's rather important. Yesterday we were served with a courtesy party of an ex parte and confidential --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, shall we go to private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm sorry. I thought we were. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We won't be long. Thank you. Now, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Salapura.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, is it your testimony that members of the 10th Diversionary Unit that participated in Branjevo Farm killings were on leave at the time of those killings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because I had received information once I arrived at the command post in Han Pijesak that the elements which had taken part in fighting back in Srebrenica had been released and allowed to go on leave. The commander had been injured and was on sick leave, and the other troops were allowed to go on leave. Only the guards remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you find that information out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th, on the evening of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did you find it from -- find it out from?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the command post that I managed to get through to one of my assistants or administrators. I can't remember quite exactly who it was that told me about that, but they said that only the three of them were still there, and that Lieutenant Colonel Karanovic had been allowed to go on leave prior to the commencement of the operation seven days early, and that Lieutenant Colonel Jankovic -- or rather, Colonel Jankovic, I think that was the rank he held at the time, that he had been sent over to the Drina Corps to act there as liaison officer, and that the detachment, the element had been involved in combat operations. The commander had been injured because a vehicle had tumbled over, and all the men had been allowed to go on leave for about ten days. I can't quite remember, but I think ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where were you when you found out about this information on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At about what time of day was this, just again roughly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was sometime in the afternoon. I really can't say. It's sort of difficult to say now what time it was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic said that Pelemis was trying to drive an UN APC and he rolled it and someone was killed. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The APC. One soldier was killed and several were injured. Pelemis himself was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So why do you think the soldiers on leave were the ones that were at Branjevo Farm? Surely not the whole 10th Diversionary Unit was on leave.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the whole unit. Half of the unit was still in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So why do you think it's the people on leave that took part in this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone else was on leave except for the guards, the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So why do you think these particular people were the ones that were at Branjevo Farm?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no inherent logic in a guard leaving his guard post. Two or three men -- the two or three men there, well, those were the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how do you know that they were even there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? Well, I don't know about that. I never said who had been at the farm, at Branjevo, wherever, or at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how do you know the 10th --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that I never referred to, and I really know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't know really who was at the Branjevo Military Farm.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't have any other information besides Drazen Erdemovic about who was at Branjevo Farm.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never looked into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know that a unit, as is customary, went to the funeral of the soldier that were killed in the 10th Diversionary after that -- after he was killed on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably someone did go, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does the name Mr. --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether anyone --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- Koljerat [phoen] ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- outside Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know, Trebinje is all the way -- as you know, all the way across Bosnia over -- all the way to --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trebinje, yes, sure. I know Trebinje. I know its location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we're probably going too fast for -- for the interpreters. Now, according to Mr. Erdemovic, he and part of his unit went all the way across Bosnia to Trebinje and were at the funeral of Mr. Koljerat on those days after the 13th but prior to going to Branjevo Farm. So they wouldn't have gone there on holiday, would they, or on leave?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know when they left for Branjevo. I don't know, or that they did go. I don't even know where Branjevo is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you a document. It's been marked as P113. If you could take a look at P113B. It's the -- I hope you can read it. This is a 17 July document under the name of Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read this. This is illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't you give it a try. It doesn't look that illegible. Are you able to make any of it out? We might have a better one now. I apologise. Yes, we do. Sir --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Wait for the better one. It's -- and it's got another number, 539.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know if it's possible to get the English on the -- on the ELMO. Is that on the ELMO? I'm sorry, I can't -- I'm not getting anything. THE USHER: It is on the ELMO. There was a technical problem. We're just sorting it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'd just like the Court to be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that. I've managed to read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to see that before today? Has anyone showed it to you or ...

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. These documents never reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, we have a little technical problem with the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, shall we proceed and -- to see how far we could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you or you ask the witness to read the relevant paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will -- I will do that. And if we could ask the audio guys to just test the -- the machines each morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'll go -- I'll go slowly. Well, first of all, do you remember any of the subject matter that -- talking about in this document? Does any of this ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the first part of it talks about - and this is to the Drina Corps Command for information -

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, audiovisual --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: - and to the 1st Zvornik Brigade, Bratunac Brigade, Miletici Brigade. And Mladic apparently in paragraph 1 is sending three officers, Colonels Nedjo Trkulja, Milovan Stankovic, and Bogdan Sladojevic, from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Do you know those three colonels?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was -- what unit was Trkulja part of?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. But what part of the Main Staff? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of armoured units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about Mr. -- or Colonel Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Stankovic was with the Ozren Operations Group. And just before that, he had come to the Main Staff, and I pointed him to -- to a post in the administration. He was sort of beginning to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Administration of intelligence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how about Bogdan Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogdan Sladojevic worked for the operational sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And are you aware that Bogdan Sladojevic had just come over from the -- the VJ to join the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he had just come from the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, he told us in an interview --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's as far as I know, as to where he came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He told us in an interview that he was on the 13th of July, 1995 a -- a member of the VJ and that on 13 July he and, I think, about 20 other officers of the VJ that were originally from Bosnia were ordered by General Perisic of the VJ to go to the VRS and become part of the VRS. You must have known about that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that when Sladojevic arrived, when the group arrived, he told me that he had been to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Now, where exactly, I didn't know. I didn't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that he was a VJ officer --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about this group of officers arriving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know we're in Courtroom I, where President -- or former President Milosevic is generally tried, but we're not into that case. I don't know what the VJ has to do with this case, with this individual at this point in time, so I think it's irrelevant. Yesterday there was a whole series of questions as to the VJ. I didn't object. But today I think -- you know, I'm always being reminded how we need to be efficient. How does the VJ -- who belonged to the VJ -- at what point in time, what does it have to do with this case? Perhaps in the Milosevic case it does. And I know we're in Courtroom I, but Mr. Milosevic isn't here and this is not his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, this is a cross-examination. I believe the Prosecution could ask any questions which might be related to the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I fail to see, Your Honour, with all due respect, how that relates to the credibility of the witness. If somebody was a member of the VJ, I just don't see the connection. But okay, if that's what he's trying to do - I don't know - I hope, maybe, perhaps, but I doubt it. I have my doubts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, your doubts is registered here, and -- and we'll see how far, you know, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- could go in this direction. But thank you very much for raising this issue. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that some 20 or more officers had just been ordered over from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of there being 20 officers who were. I know that some officers came over. Whether that was pursuant to an order or whatever, this is something I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's not --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there had been an order, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's not worry about the numbers, then. So -- but you were aware that several VJ officers came over to be part of the VRS at this time period, around 13 July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know when exactly this was, whether in June or in May. That's when they came. I'm not sure when precisely Sladojevic came. I can't give you the exact date. It's been nine years. It would not be fair to start guessing now, whether it was back in 1994 or 1995, what the time frame was, and when the whole thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Don't worry about the dates. As I've said, you know roughly the time period we're talking about that VJ officers came over to be part of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it was in that period or in what period it was. Those men, Sladojevic and I'm not sure who else had arrived, but there were other persons who had arrived, or how many. I don't know. This is something I can't say, and I can't specify the time period, whether it was this day or that day. I can't give you the exact date or time of their arrival, even if we're talking about years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go for one more question on this into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in paragraph 3, it talks about Lieutenant Colonel Keserovic getting appointed to the various units that were combing the territory for the remaining Muslim forces. Who is Lieutenant Colonel Keserovic at the time and what was his position?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Lieutenant Colonel Keserovic at the time, he was with the military police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the last word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I believe later he came to the Main Staff as an administrator. Whether it was before or after -- but if you look at this order, then probably it was prior to this. Before all this happened, but I can't say exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were in Han Pijesak at the time of this order, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 17th I was in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've seen this intercept, which I won't go over in detail, that was P265, where your name is mentioned, Keserovic is mentioned. Do you know -- but you don't know anything about that intercept or this order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can't see anything from that, and I'm not sure what the context is. I've said before and I'll say it again. I spent most of my time in bed recovering at the time. I would go up to the room occasionally, but I didn't go out very often on the 18th and the 17th. That's one thing I know for sure. In the morning, I went to see a doctor. I was feeling slightly better and I had been receiving therapy. And on the 18th, on the afternoon of the 18th, I drove back to Banja Luka, because on the 17th we had received word that the road was again open for traffic. As for Karanovic, the analyst, that was on the 17th, I think, but I can't say. I think it was on that day that he was back from leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before you left --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, well, as for the telex, I really can't make any sense of that. So I can't see the name of the document and I have no idea what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before you left for Banja Luka, had you heard about the over five or 6.000 Muslim prisoners that had been murdered in the Bratunac and Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you on the morning of the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you -- you testified earlier that you did contact the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I told you. I just didn't tell you whether it's the 15th. I cannot say exactly which date it is. Or is it the 16th? Perhaps if you have some documents that could jog my memory. So that's what happened. The information came before the counter-attack that the Muslim forces were supposed to carry out from Tuzla vis-a-vis some particular facility, but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if we use the very early morning hours of the 16th of July as the -- the morning the Muslim forces surged across Serb lines and killed more than 50 Serb soldiers, would it have occurred -- would you have been contacting Zvornik prior to that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's asking the gentleman to speculate, Your Honour. I don't object to the question, but it is rather speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't think so, because there's some basis there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I'm just -- I'm just suggesting that it might be speculative. I don't object to the question, you know, to the form -- to the nature of the question, but the form, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, I'm just trying to -- you've indicated it might have been the 14th, 15th, or even the 16th, so I'm just trying to help you narrow the date a bit. So we know, and I'm sure you remember, that -- that morning of 16 July during that battle, but -- so can you tell us at -- roughly how long before that horrible morning that you were in contact with the Zvornik Brigade ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I really can't say. It's been quite a while, hasn't it? I can just guess. I mean, it must have been before that. I know that I consider that to be an important piece of information and an urgent piece of information that should be forwarded to the command. As for the exact date, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat what you just said. The interpreters missed that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be an attack, a counter-attack from the direction of Tuzla. It would be carried out by the forces of the Tuzla Corps and the attack would be against a particular facility. I don't know exactly which one. But this is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And where did you go to actually communicate with the Zvornik Brigade? Where -- what part of the facility at Han Pijesak did you go to communicate?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go anywhere. I just walked out of the room where my analysts were working, out of the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: To where? To the radio room?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. I had a room of my own where I was lying down, and that's where I had a telephone. But I had a big room where the analysts were working, with several desks, and that's where the telephone links were, and that is where one could establish communication with different units, different elements, the Drina Corps. I don't know exactly the ways in which these communications would be established. I mean, I cannot define that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to pick up your phone and contact the Drina Corps, who patched you through to Zvornik, as is, we've learned to be, the normal way ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd have to call the switchboard, our switchboard at the Main Staff, and then I'd have to ask them to put me through to the Drina Corps, and then to ask from the Drina Corps to put me through to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you remember that happened on one of these days, 14, 15 July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to this document. It's the duty officer notebook, P507. As was mentioned yesterday, sir, this is the rough notes of the duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade that he scratched down as he got information and various calls. And I want to ask you: Did you know -- and I think you've spoken about this before, but did you know a Major Pavle Golic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. Of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was his -- what unit was he in and what was his position?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an officer in the intelligence department of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So he was someone you were very acquainted with.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you say "operations" yesterday, or am I misrecollecting that? I thought you said he was in operations, or maybe it was a translation error .

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sorry, I never said that. I couldn't have possibly said something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He told us that he was in the -- in the intel branch, like you say, so I just wanted to clear that up. Now, are you aware of a Lieutenant Drago Nikolic from the Zvornik Brigade, the chief of security?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Drago. I think I met him in 1992. I saw him two or three times, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And now, if you will look at this conversation, and figuring that the Colonel Salapura is you, Drago is Lieutenant Drago Nikolic, Beara is Colonel Ljubisa Beara --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and Golic is Pavle Golic. Now, Golic was at the Drina Corps Command on the -- on the 14th of July, as far as we know. Do you have any reason to believe he was somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I really cannot say anything to you on the basis of this: I really do not remember. I can just engage in guesswork now. But if you want me to engage in guesswork and assumptions, then I can give you 100 options, and then we can see what would come out of that. The only thing I can tell you now is what I told you already; namely, that I cannot give orders either to Beara or Nikolic. That is quite clear. Pajo Golic particularly cannot. I know that for sure. So this was just a transfer of information from one person to another, from superiors. That's the only thing that could have happened, taking a message, something like that. On the basis of this, it is impossible to say anything. I can just guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I just asked you if you knew where Golic was. I didn't ask you to guess. I don't want you to guess. And so if you don't know, that's fine. So you say this --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at that particular moment. I cannot tell you where the man was at that particular moment. Perhaps he was in the office; perhaps he was in town; perhaps he was, I don't know, in Zvornik, in Vlasenica. I don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let me give you some facts, and maybe it will refresh your recollection, but you said you think this was just merely information, you know, passed from one to another, and I -- I think that's right. That's what it looks like. So do you have any reason to doubt this, that you -- that you called and -- and gave the message that Drago and Beara were supposed to report to Golic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I'd have to guess. Well, we can guess. I've already said so. There's a hundred options that are possible. But after all this time to remember such details --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't want you to guess. You're the one that said this is just information being passed from one to another. Now, I'm asking you: Is there any reason to believe this didn't happen, that you called these guys and just passed on this information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that it was only passing on information. I'm telling you I cannot remember. I cannot remember what exactly happened. I just gave you one of the possible options.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me give you what the facts have shown here. Maybe it will help your -- refresh your recollection. Okay, Colonel Salapura, you are at Han Pijesak, the Main Staff headquarters. You are the head intel man under Tolimir. You have been to the area, talked to officers, including Mladic and others. You should be briefed on what's going on. Now, you call. From the headquarters you get patched through from Vlasenica to Zvornik, you speak to the duty officer, and you tell that duty officer basically that Drago Nikolic and Colonel Beara should report --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry, do you mean by telephone?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's -- by telephone or by radio, however you would normally communicate.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that you told the duty officer to -- to have Drago Nikolic and Ljubisa Beara report to Major Pavle Golic of the intel branch, who would be in Vlasenica that morning of the 14th. Now, the morning of the 14th, Drago Nikolic was arranging for prisoners, some five, 6.000 prisoners that were located in some four schools all over the Zvornik area and preparing for their execution. Beara was doing the same thing, first in Bratunac, then in Zvornik on the 14th. And we know that Pavle Golic was involved in that process because we know from an intercept that he is assisting in providing 500 litres of fuel to buses on the 16th of July from Mr. Popovic to transport prisoners around Pilica. So given that background, does that help refresh your recollection about why you would have been calling and asking the duty officer to have Drago Nikolic and Ljubisa Beara report to your subordinate, Major Pavle Golic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I did not have anything that would be pointing to such activities, not a hint. As for what this is about specifically, I could not say. I did not have a single hint, as I've already said, that would point to such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do, just brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have a few questions. The information that you received --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could get the assistants to lower the -- thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The information that you received from Belgrade, did you consider that serious information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And during that period of time, what were your main focuses? What were you focussing on, being the intel person? What areas?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the western part. As an intelligence person as at the Main Staff, only the western part. As for this zone, in the eastern part, that was the task of the corps and of their intelligence organs .

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, which part are we -- which part is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This has been gone through, and it's really not contested --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is not just a green light to go into the material all over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The suggestion was why didn't this gentleman go to track down prisoners in Nova Kasaba to talk to them. This is the highest ranking officer in the intel. And I'm trying to show that there is a reason why in the areas in which he was focussing, because there was a huge suggestion being made that somehow this individual should have been tracking down where the 28th Column was, and that's why I'm trying to refocus the gentleman. It will be five minutes and we can all get on to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I understand that the parties have different views on that, and I believe that we have -- already know, you know, your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you were questioned about your connections with the VJ as if you were a member of the Yugoslav army or had connections with the Milosevic government at that point in time. Could you please tell us whether you had travelled to other places, such as the Federation or Croatia or other countries, to meet with sources to get intelligence information on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did travel to the area of the Federation for negotiations, talks, et cetera, but this is an area, Your Honours, that I think is not really relevant to this particular trial. I did travel, and also the operations people involved in this particular line of work. We travelled abroad too, to Hungary and to other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That was --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that means anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That does mean quite a bit. Thank you. Now, had General Mladic taken the information that you had been trying to convey to him seriously, would that have changed the course of events, perhaps later on, in what -- what happened in the Krajina area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. These are just open-ended -- this is a great concern to the Prosecution because we don't have the Rules -- under the Rules re-cross, and this is not rebuttal, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know if there's going to be a long explanation and -- and all that in front of the witness, I would prefer that the witness be -- be left out. But it's very simple to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I can, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: --rephrase the question .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think this is a hypothetical question, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday the Prosecution was trying to suggest that you didn't care about the Serb soldiers that were ultimately killed in -- by the 28th Division in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know, in -- in telling this witness what the Prosecution thinks about him, this is just absurd and inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is what he was trying to suggest, Your Honour, that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have come over -- we have come over this issue many, many, many times in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was the suggestion, Your Honour, that I -- I gleaned from the line of the questioning. And now I'm trying to suggest that he was also concerned about other lies, a potential onslaught that was about to happen and did in fact happen, and had Mladic listened to him, perhaps, you know, things could have been avoided. That's what I'm trying to suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may ask the questions in -- based on that "yesterday you were asked a question," so on and so forth, "what's your view about it?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I'm going to need to explain now what I was -- I was trying to suggest that this man would have been concerned about those Serb lives and as a result would have known about information in the column, not that he wouldn't have been concerned about Serb lives. That's absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At the point in time when you met General Mladic and you were trying to convey the information that you had learned from Belgrade, what were you concerned about? Which area and for what events?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For quite a while I only dealt with the western area, the HVO and the preparation of the Croatian forces for an attack and, of course, the forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their preparations in Trebinje, so that area in Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say, I focussed on the western part. My approach to all these problems was selective, because I had very few people available. You could have seen that in the Srebrenica operation. The key people were absent; they were not present at all in that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Incidentally, did your source, the one that you met in Belgrade, tell you what we learned in this courtroom, that the HVO at the time had been receiving arms from the United States and other countries in preparation for this particular activity?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is really going beyond anything, and it's obviously deliberate. That -- and it cuts to the foundation of this adversarial system, which I'm ready to give up on, frankly, but it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Because I'm going to need to have re-cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He's more than welcome to have re-cross, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think this question is out of scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please drop it .

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me go back to a document that was shown to you by the Prosecutor. It's P865.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could have the assistance of -- I only have my English version, so I suspect that perhaps -- oh, here's the B/C/S. I apologise. Here we go. And we could put my copy on the ELMO here so we can all see it. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you please look at -- you told us that General Tolimir was both the head of intelligence and security at that point in time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Chief of Sector for Intelligence and Security Affairs, and at the same time he was deputy -- or rather, assistant commander for these particular affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there a time -- do we see a time on this particular document? We see a date, 13 July.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at -- look at the document closely. I don't have my copy. "2230 hours," at the top -- at the very top on the right-hand, do you see where it says " 2230 hours"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just not sure who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I'm correct, would that be 10.30 at night, July 13th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from looking at this particular document that was shown to you by the Prosecution yesterday, would it not appear that General Tolimir is suggesting that prisoners be sent and be put up in places where usually Serb officers -- or Serb soldiers stay and to work -- to do this agricultural work? Is that what he is suggesting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at this document, that's what it says; clearly, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can you conclude from this document whether at that point in time General Tolimir, who was both the head of the security and intelligence sector, would have known about any killing operations on -- on the 13th of July at 10.30 p.m. that night?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This witness says he doesn't know anything about this document, and this is -- nor does he know much about anything, so this has to be speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- well, it is a speculative question because, you know, this document was issued by another person and we ask this witness to tell us what's in the mind of that person. But -- but in this circumstances, I would like to hear the answer from this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can read this document. I can have a look, just like you can. What it says is perfectly clear. I'm not sure what the problem is. It talks about the existing capacities for putting people up and then about these 800 or perhaps 80 prisoners of war, because I can't read clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me just rephrase my question. There's been testimony here by Momir Nikolic that on the morning of the 12th he was informed by Popovic and Kosoric that all of the men were to be separated and killed. Looking at this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're now going, you know, way out again, into other witnesses, other testimony. You know, if he'd chosen this tact on -- on direct, but how that has to do with -- with this getting -- speculation on this document is pretty far-fetched.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This document was introduced by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have any problems with him questioning about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm questioning the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think the issue about this document has already been solved. This witness answered the question, and we are satisfied with this answer. Shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we can move on. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two questions, Your Honour. Good morning, first of all, Mr. Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the cross-examination yesterday at one point you stated that the job of a unit intelligence officer was to interview prisoners in order to gather intelligence. You remember that; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the context of the question, you were asked why were you not the one who was interviewing those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As an officer attached to the Main Staff, it wasn't your job to do that sort of thing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As chief, I certainly wasn't expected to interview prisoners of war. It wouldn't even have been an operational kind of job; although, I did that sort of job, because I was short of staff. But that's a different question altogether. It's more a complex one. Whereas, this is something that anyone can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's precisely in that context that I want to ask you the following: Hypothetically speaking, an intelligence officer attached to the command of the Zvornik Brigade, Dusko Vukotic, receives information that he is to interview a prisoner of war. He is duty-bound to do it. And would I be right in stating the following: Once he has gathered the necessary intelligence, the prisoner of war belongs to the security organ who should then process the prisoner, as far as the operational aspect is concerned? It would not be the duty of the intelligence officer, would it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By no means would that be the job of an intelligence officer. Each unit's commander determines the gathering place, a spot where the prisoners of war are gathered and secured. The next step is camps are determined and all the other logistics organs and security organs get involved. The whole security system, how security is provided, taking the prisoners there, the involvement of the police units, and so on and so forth. But this is something that the commander determines in his order. As for the unit intelligence officer, the intelligence officer that's attached to the unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just please slow down for the benefit of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intelligence officer attached to a certain unit only comes up with a request to interview a particular prisoner, if the prisoner is suspected to contain essential information, to be in possession of essential information, if there is the possibility that the prisoner may be in possession of relevant information. Only in that case, because that's relevant to security and to escorting the prisoners. Now, whichever unit is in charge, intelligence or security, they must turn to the superior commander for approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the next question I have, something you said today on cross-examination, that you personally in the morning on the 14th had no information whatsoever concerning the activities of Ljubisa Beara and Dragan Nikolic over those days in the area covered by the Zvornik Brigade. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So even if you had wanted to, you would have been in no position to inform the person that you may have contacted at the command of the Zvornik Brigade as to why, on which mission precisely those two persons were in the Zvornik area to begin with.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's certain. I didn't even know they were there. There could have been possibly a message that had been conveyed, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the job of the duty operations officer would be to pass the message on.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, just as much to pass it on. The message could have been received, for example, by the duty operations officer at the Main Staff receiving the message and saying, "Pass it on to Salapura and he should call such and such person for this or for that," or it could have been any other officer there. Based on that, you can't tell who the message came from or who it was passed on by. It's very difficult for me to say so many years later what exactly had taken place, because there are a number of different possibilities, hundreds of them, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for you. Your Honours, this completes my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Salapura. I have some questions for you. Can you explain us the functional differences between intelligence bodies, security bodies, and military police in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence bodies, as any other intelligence bodies, what they do is only collecting, gathering intelligence on the enemy forces, the sort of terrain they are dealing with; and with regard to the other side of the front and enemy-controlled territory, of course, that sort of intelligence. As for security organs, they deal with security-related and counter-intelligence-related issues. In our territory, in enemy-controlled territory, and they apply the overall security system. They propose measures to the commander, and they monitor the implementation of those measures. The military police are a unit with their own special tasks. I'm not sure if I am able to list those in details. They deal with security. They take part in combat, monitoring, escort, traffic, providing security for facilities and persons, for camps, for prisons, and so on and so forth, everything that happens at army level, or the tribunal, as the police do here. Well, they have the same sort of authority as the police. Only in zones covered by military units and in relation to military personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My next question: What units or elements of the VRS were charged to deal with and care of prisoners of war and enemies, refugees?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. Taking prisoners to the camps and providing security there, above all, the military police units and the police units would be in charge of that. If that proves insufficient - I'm talking about rules about the general principles, what is envisaged as a rule - the commander may choose to appoint any other unit, even a unit not taking part in combat activities at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what was the role of intelligence bodies and security bodies in providing, let us say, care of prisoners of war? Or in dealing with prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence bodies have no jurisdiction over that, except if the need arises for them to make a request. If they are in a camp, from the camp command to perhaps interview one of the prisoners in order to gather specific intelligence, or while a prisoner is being captured, if there is an officer, a battalion officer who realises that this person may be in possession of certain relevant information, they can call the battalion's intelligence administrator, who will then gather the information on the spot, which unit the person belongs to, where the unit was located. But that's the only authority that the intelligence bodies have over prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What about security bodies?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security bodies regulate a whole number of different things: Taking the prisoners there, providing security, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And military police? What is the role of military police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, security bodies make proposals, which forces should be involved. That's up to the commanders, whether it should be the military police, police units, some other units perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Okay. My next question: What was the --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said -- my apologies. My apologies. That wasn't part of my job, the security detail. I'm no expert in that field. I'm not familiar with details. But generally speaking, that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the chain of command in relation to security bodies and intelligence bodies in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only talk about intelligence-related matters. Intelligence bodies did not really have a centralised structure. At Main Staff level, there was an administration, an administration which had its own departments, and it was poorly staffed. This is something that I could never successfully deal with. I couldn't find a solution. It had operational officers, who gathered operational intelligence. So much for the administration. We had a unit attached section [as interpreted] and intelligence officers who were attached to units, and they were only responsible to their own commanders and Chiefs of Staff. The administration had no authority to exercise command over them or to give them orders. They were duty-bound to submit intelligence to the administration and the administration would then pass intelligence on to corps-level bodies such information as they had. Once it has been processed, it would be passed on so it could be used. And all this would be envisaged in an order on intelligence and security. The administration dealt with training those people, getting them to have proper qualifications for their work, and it also issued directives on how their work should be improved. If there was something that had to be done pursuant to a request made by the administration, then the administration had to make this request and to send it to the Chief of Staff at corps level, so that the Chief of Staff could then approve a possible involvement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, as far as I know, in some units of the VRS - for example, in the Bratunac Brigade - the security and intelligence functions were performed by one person. Whom this person was subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person was subordinated to the brigade commander -- or rather, to the Chief of Staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what about his superiors in the, let us say, chain -- security and intelligence chain?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have the corps, the intelligence organ -- or rather, the security organ of the corps, but the corps intelligence organ can only submit their own information, and it is duty-bound to pass their intelligence on to the corps intelligence organ. It can't give it orders. That is under sole jurisdiction of the brigade staff, Chief of Staff, as far as intelligence work is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My last question: Whose orders could have precedence for the brigade security and intelligence officer? Those issued by, for example, Colonel Beara and orders of brigade commander, provided they had the same subject matter.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a question for security organs, not for me, I believe. They have their own methods, methods that my units didn't use. They have their own communication structure, methods of reporting and briefing. What my service did was totally transparent. Everyone received our information, the Chiefs of Staffs, commands, and their information was submitted in a different way, through different channels. This is something that I don't feel competent to talk about. I think you should ask someone who does this sort of job, because I could only be speculating at best. It's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's question? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you are not -- well, Mr. Kosoric being the Drina Corps chief intel officer; right? Svetozar Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were not his commander. You wouldn't issue him orders.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's the commander, Chief of Staff, his commander, corps commander. He was a unit intelligence officer with the corps. All I could do -- or rather, what I was duty-bound to do is to pass information on to him and then his duty was to pass information on to the administration. I may have told him, for example, that he wasn't doing his job well enough, and my analysts, who'd come up with proposals as to what should be improved, we could organise training session, a seminar perhaps, get people in to talk about these things, to explain things. That would have been the jurisdiction of the administration over that. The commander was authorised, for example, to -- to get an intelligence officer and appoint him to act as battalion commander for a month, or for 20 days. There were cases like that, many. We had an intelligence officer with the corps who spent six months working as the chief of the operations group. That's up to the commander. This is something that I -- that I had no authority over. I wasn't there to issue tasks for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The commander, be it the corps, brigade, or Main Staff, is central to all this in the exercise of command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All what, Your Honour? All this regarding intelligence, I take it? I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He knows what I'm talking about, and he answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would expect Mr. McCloskey to show a little more respect. I understand he's a little afraid lately, but, you know, he could be respectful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the context is very clear here in the answers and the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just hope that tu quoque applies in this area, if he's going to be behaving this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I do not see anything abnormal, you know, happened here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura and I are having a good discussion. Unfortunately, the answer was interrupted by counsel and it didn't get on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe you could re-ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Salapura, in this -- what you've been discussing, the -- the relationship between the intel branches and command, command is central to this entire process and this entire decision-making process, isn't it, the commander's role?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander takes the decisions and he's the one who gives orders, and he's the one who bears all the responsibility for -- for the overall implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the responsibility of command.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what you said, your relationship with Kosoric is just as true with Kosoric's relationship with Momir Nikolic; is that correct? The Main Staff to corps and the corps to brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, we lose something there. Your question is: "So that's the responsibility of commander." I think the witness answered that question, but we did not pick it up in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: It doesn't appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps I interrupted that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Go slowly. We still have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, so my question was: The commander is central to this role in making the decisions.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what you described -- your relationship with Kosoric is it works the same way between Mr. Kosoric and the corps and Mr. Momir Nikolic in the brigade; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the intelligence line. Absolutely. Intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have described the security line to us briefly, and you have stated that the security officers also report to their commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to -- I'm going to object at this point. He's indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. First of all, it's a mischaracterisation, a gross one at that. Secondly, the gentleman indicated that he's not competent. Thirdly, we have a security, you know, general coming in next and he can ask those questions of -- of that. But the gentleman indicated that he wasn't competent in that field. He's also indicated that they're separate branches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I -- I believe that the witness will say something to us. Let the witness tell us. Witness, are you going to say something? Are you going to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said I was talking about everything that was intelligence related. As for security, I'm no expert in that field. I'm not qualified to talk about that. So that's all I'm talking about, but that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're familiar with the rules, and you testified in direct that security officers also report to their commanders. You know that much.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Certainly the commander is responsible for the military police platoons and units under his command.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's responsible for everything that is under his command, all units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, at this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. D194/1, which is the intelligence information; D195/1, another intelligence information; D196/1, intelligence information; D197, an intercept. And in the eventuality the Prosecution does not introduce P865, we would like to tender it as D199. We believe it demonstrates Mr. Tolimir's state of mind at the time and what his knowledge was with respect to whether any execution plans were underway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. But I should -- I should note, also if we could get those intercepts -- you've heard a lot about Bosnian Muslim intercepts. These -- just as for background on authentication, the intercept referred to by Mr. Karnavas was obtained in a search of a -- I believe it was a Bosnian Croat military facility, and we have -- do not have -- have not been able to conduct the thorough investigation of those materials that we have on the others. There are -- yeah, it was in Mostar. There are, in fact, three sort of synopses of conversations on this intercept. Mr. Salapura has actually spoken of the content of the last one, and I think that is self-authenticating to that degree, because he recalled that information. And so the other two I just wanted to let the Court know that yes, you may -- I have no objection to this coming in, but we do not -- do not know the processes and the people and how they were all conducted, but I think given his testimony, that certainly the third intercept should -- should be admitted, and I have no objection to the other two coming in as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And would you please indicate to us the -- the number of that intercept. Here we have several. That is D197?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think since there's no objections from the Prosecution, those documents are admitted into the evidence; although, we don't believe that the D194 is relevant. Maybe in the future we could see the relevance by reading other documents, but at this stage those documents are admitted into the evidence. On the part of the Prosecution, do you have any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I -- just the one document counsel referred to, P865, the Tolimir document. And he made a brief argument on that document. And if I could be allowed 20 seconds to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, I don't think it's proper, you know. Are you -- are you going to tell us about the background of this document or the source of this document or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was going to respond to Mr. Karnavas's argument, but I wanted to get your leave to do it, because I agree with you, it's not proper at this stage to be making an argument. But I think given that counsel has made an argument, I could take 20 seconds just to alert you to something in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, he just indicated that it's improper for him to make an argument, so I hope -- you know, I don't understand what his problem is. He can offer the document or not. If he's not going to offer it, I would like to offer it. If he wants to make an argument, there'll be plenty of time in closing argument for him to make an argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you oppose it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's necessary, but I'm not -- you know, I leave it to the Court's discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, since there is opposition from Defence, I think we have to stick to the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The document P865 is admitted into evidence, maybe with the two numbers, one is for Prosecution and the other is for the Defence. It is so decided. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. We wish you have a pleasant journey back home. When we are adjourned, the usher will show you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we are adjourned now, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karnavas, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragomir Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us your last name letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: K-e-s-e-r-o-v-i-c, with a diacritic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. Could you please tell us, what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Currently I am a general in the Army of Republika Srpska, and I hold the position of Assistant Minister of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what is the area of your expertise within the VRS.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I am head of the Department of Security -- or rather, head of the Security Service of Defence in the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how long have you held that position, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Since the 10th of September, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could just briefly discuss your educational background. Could you tell us after completing secondary education what sort of education -- further education, higher education you received.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I completed the military Academy for Ground Forces Armoured Units in 1981. I completed the General Staff Academy in Belgrade and the Army of Yugoslavia in 1997. From the 1st of February, 1996 until the 1st of February, 1997, that is. I completed the School of National Defence, also in Belgrade, in the school year of 1998-1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: As far as the military is concerned, I completed many educational courses that have to do with the Security Service and the military police. I also completed a post-graduate course at the Faculty of National Defence, again within the Department of Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, could you please tell us back in July 1995 what rank you had within the VRS.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us in which organ or in which capacity you were serving.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was in the military police department of the security administration of the sector for security and intelligence affairs of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where were you located at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of my department was in Banja Luka in the building of the headquarters of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you have any -- anything to do with the 65 Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Not with the regiment. But like with the other units of the Army of Republika Srpska, I had professional links with the battalion of the military police from the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please describe to us in general those professional links.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The security department worked on training and equipping military police units. It worked on the seven services of the military police too, and it also worked on giving guidance to the duty services of the military police. Those are the three directions of activity within the military police. From a professional point of view, that was channelled by the military police department from the security administration, from the Sector for Intelligence and Security Affairs of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You said that you worked on the seven services of the military police. Could you please describe to us in general what those seven services are.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I think I can do that. That is the service for providing security, then the investigation service, the patrol service, the escort service, the duty service, the service for crime prevention and control, and the service for the control of military traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us, in light of your position during that period of time - and I'm speaking of July 1995 in general - what was your professional affiliation or link with Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Beara was the chief of the security administration. In that administration, there were four organisational entities. One of them was the department for Military Police, and I was in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just so we -- we have a clear understanding, you said that there were four organisational entities. Could you list the other two.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The other three: The counter-intelligence department, the analysis department, and the counter-intelligence group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then the military police being the fourth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was -- who was your immediate superior officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it he would be the one giving you orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It can be put that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- well, did you report to anyone directly, other than Beara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you have a staff of your own?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Not in the department. Until I came to the military police department, it only existed on paper, and there was not a single person who was involved in military police affairs. At the time when I was in that department, I was there by myself. So after I left, no one stayed behind. It was only later that it was manned. So in the department itself, I did not have anyone who would work with me on these particular affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was -- specifically or concretely, what was the military police department -- or what were you in charge of in your capacity as the head of the military police department?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, we were primarily involved in manning military police units and providing appropriate personnel, since there weren't enough personnel. Also, we tried to equip the units with appropriate materiel and technical equipment, and we were making efforts to bring military police units into a position so that they would not be classical military units, as they were primarily until then, but we wanted them to carry out specific military police duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, to what extent did your position reach down all the way, say, to the brigade level?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: There were criteria according to which this manning took place and according to which both personnel and equipment were sent to particular units and also members of military police units were sent for training according to certain criteria. Recruitment was centralised, and we took part in the decision-making process as to how many soldiers should be sent to which units. Procurement was centralised too. Military police equipment was procured, and then we suggested how it should further be allocated to different units. Then we also linked up the duty services from the brigade through the corps, all the way to the battalion of the military police in the Motorised Protection Regiment. These were links that were based on the legislation and rules that were in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
