utterances.text: Now, at your level, would you be able to influence, say, a brigade as to who would be placed in the military police, who would command it, who would be the deputy commander, the numbers, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I could not decide, I did not have the right to decide, but there was a rule that the commander of a unit when deciding to appoint officers to the military police should consult first and foremost his own security organ and then, if necessary, the superior officer in the military police chain. It could happen that the opinion of the corps would be sought for appointing a military police officer in the battalion, but this hardly ever happened in the case of companies and squads, but then it depends on where they were too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in light of your -- in light of your position, I take it you had to work with the rules and regulations dealing with the security organ in general. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. But there are two sets of rules involved, and as you said, generally speaking all members of the security organs were supposed to adhere to them at all levels, regardless of their position and their actual line of work. One set of these rules is the rules of service in the security organs, and the second set are the rules of service of the military police, the instructions for applying the rules of the military police, and the laws that accompany these rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I want to speak at the -- at the brigade level, the relationship, you know, between the security organ and the commander, or how the security organ fits within the command. Could you please describe to us in general what were the general -- what were the functions of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: A security organ is a member of the brigade command and is one of the assistant commanders too. As for his work, in terms of the security of the unit, he is responsible to the brigade commander. At the same time, he takes part in the work of the brigade command in the process of planning and adopting decisions. In that context, he proposes measures related to security and using the military police unit that may be within the composition of that unit. That is his relationship vis-a-vis the brigade commander. The security organ of a brigade has another link, which is professional -- or rather, functional. It is called professional command and control, and that is vis-a-vis the superior security organ -- or rather, the head of the superior security organ. As regards these matters that have to do with professional command and control, most often this is counter-intelligence, the security organ is responsible to the superior security organ and only to a certain extent that he or the responsible security organ believe it is necessary, so it is only to that extent that he familiarises the brigade commander with that particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, I want to go into a little more detail on this aspect which you just covered. When you say, "Professional command and control," could you please describe to us, to the best that you can, concretely, that is, what are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: When we say "professional command and control" in the Security Service, this entails many activities, mostly from the so-called counter-intelligence area of activity. There are two elements that are important in terms of understanding this: The first is that the security organ in a certain period of time deals with information, data, assessments, and evaluations of security challenges, risks, and threats within the unit and addressed against the unit that were not expressed very evidently, so they do not have enough valid evidence yet. They cannot inform the commander and the others as yet about this, and also ultimately this may lead to criminal prosecution before courts of law. That is one side of it -- or rather, one element. The second one is the following: When following these activities and documenting them, the law prescribes the methods and means according to which the principle of the inviolability of public information and communication is deviated from. On the basis of special authority and powers that security organs have, this falls under this professional command and control and the professional line of work they are engaged in in a particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these two elements, did you just give us a definition of what is considered counter-intelligence? Was that what that was -- the two elements that you were describing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, is there anything else about counter-intelligence that we should know about in trying to understand this concept, what is counter-intelligence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: There is a broad spectrum of security threats. There are many ways in which the enemy tries to endanger a unit. Sometimes this happens within the unit itself; sometimes it happens in such a way that it involves foreign elements. This also has to do with the protection of confidential or secret military information at all levels, secrecy of decisions. And also according to the rules that regulate this particular matter, then there is activity related to opposing foreign intelligence services, also activity involving internal undermining. Then -- then there is the possibility of paramilitary organisations within the area or the unit itself. All of that are concrete counter-intelligence affairs that have to be followed, monitored, documented, and this should lead to an epilogue that is prescribed by law in one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at which level -- or at what level, I should say, is counter-intelligence determined within the security organ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me be a little more concrete. Would the -- would a security officer at the battalion level, would he make a decision as to what is or is not counter-intelligence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: He does not make decisions as to what counter-intelligence activity is, because counter-intelligence activity is precisely spelled out in the instructions and the rules. However, he does register activities and collect information which he deems to be of security interest and which he feels may jeopardise his unit, the unit he is in at a given point in time. When information is collected in this way, he sends it further on to the superior security organ, who re-evaluates this information, and then professionally he gives guidance to the lower-level security organ, in terms of what he should do with regard to a particular matter. He himself does not always decide what he is going to do next. In most cases, he is given professional guidance by the superior security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, would -- before seeking this -- this guidance by the superior security organ, this professional guidance, could the security officer of a battalion go directly to his battalion commander to seek some guidance or at least pass on that information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, the answer is yes. There are a few serious security issues that can occur at battalion level that would require the superior security organ to be consulted before you go and talk to your own commander, but it's very difficult to remember any practical example, but certainly there are a few such problems, because all problems that are likely to happen, to occur at battalion level, for the most part are problems of a more public nature, and one could say that it is possible to go and confer with the battalion commander. Of course, if one is looking at the kind of information or data that could spread and become a more general security problem and the battalion-level security organ is then able to consider all of the potential consequences and predict how the situation might evolve surrounding that problem, the rule is first one goes to the superior security organ, confers with him and receives instructions as to what to do next. However, when serious problems are encountered, first you go to the superior security organ. If it's a problem of a more public nature and easier to spot and identify and document, then one can go directly to one's own unit commander, and the unit commander, under all aspects of combat readiness, is the responsible one, and this organ is there to help with security-related issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's move up to the brigade, the brigade level. And now we're talking about the brigade security organ. With respect to activities or information collected within the sphere of counter-intelligence, to whom would the security organ first and foremost inform or report to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In the sense of security regarding the staff -- or rather, one part of the activity, roughly speaking, one-third of the overall activity undertaken by security organs in a given command, this would be up to the unit commander, to the brigade commander only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the other two-thirds?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: As for the remaining two-thirds, that merits a brief explanation, but the remaining two-thirds constitute the so-called counter-intelligence activities and tasks, and that is the focus of the work of security organs. As I said before, in that respect, the security organ is, professionally speaking, under the command and control of a superior officer, in the security organ itself. The security organ goes about these tasks and activities without necessarily informing the brigade commander every single time. They do provide some sort of general information as to their potential whereabouts or the general nature of certain tasks and duties in the sphere of counter-intelligence-related activity, or perhaps not even that much; they can only say, "I have some jobs and duties that I have to carry out personally or pursuant to an order from the security organ," and now a professionally trained commander will not ask any further questions of the security organ at this point. Once the results of that work become apparent and once it is possible to prove these results, then the security organ has the duty to inform the unit commander accordingly. In some way, as far as the relations between the commander and the security organ, it has always been the stumbling-block of the exact ratio and the amount of reporting and information that was supposed to go on. This is a matter of one's assessment. This is a matter of the training level of the security organ itself, as well as the trust that has been established between the organ and the commander. However, the correct way to do it would be to inform the commander so that the commander or the unit would not be liable to any surprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at the brigade level, the superior security organ for a brigade security officer would be where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: That is the chief of the security and intelligence or intelligence and security-related tasks with the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that at some point there would be a duty if and when the time came for the security officer or the head of the security for the brigade to inform his commander about those counter-intelligence activities. My question is: Would he take that decision on his own, or would he need some sort of approval or guidance from the superior security organ prior to disclosing the information that he had -- or the work that he had been conducting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, it's leading. The question should be what advice, if any, does a person need to take, not offering a potential answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may rephrase your question, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. But the way that Mr. McCloskey stated it doesn't make any sense, so I'm afraid I can't ask it in that fashion. Because that wasn't the purpose of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to ask your question according to the Prosecution's fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: After conducting this counter-intelligence activity -- or actually, before the security organ at the brigade level can inform the commander of his activities or information gathered from counter-intelligence activities, does he need to get permission, and if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: A combined method of work or an operational combined method of work is a very complex activity indeed. It is very difficult to provide a brief answer to that question. However, in most cases, the superior officer of the security organ can provide recommendations and advice to his subordinates as to what extent exactly the brigade commander should be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What would be the relationship, if there exists one, between the security organ of the brigade, at the brigade level, with the security organ at the Main Staff level?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: There is no direct relationship. Only through the officers of the corps security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you concretely, just to make sure that I understand it. Is there a direct relationship between Beara, who was at the Main Staff, and Momir Nikolic at the Bratunac Brigade? In other words, can Beara or should Beara, under the rules, assuming that they are followed, go directly to Nikolic and give him orders, advice, directions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How should it work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: As long as the tasks arise from assessments and evaluations at the level of the security administration attached to the Main Staff, these should then be sent to the chief of the corps department, and the chief of the corps department should pass them on to the section chief in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about the reverse scenario? Can Nikolic, or should Nikolic, assuming that the rules are followed, go directly to Beara, bypassing, in other words, Popovic, who's at the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what about -- what about the general himself, Mladic? Can he, assuming the rules as they were designed to be applied, can he, given his position, being the commander of the VRS, go and directly give an order to Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: To all practical intents and purposes, this could be the case but this is not the correct way to do it. The correct way to do it would be for General Mladic to go to his assistant - specifically, General Tolimir - give him a task, and then the task is passed on down the line of communication that we have already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what if the general was in the vicinity, General Mladic? Again, now the reverse. Would Momir Nikolic be entitled to go, under the rules, directly to General Mladic to give him some sort of a security or intelligence report, in light of his position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: At this point, this is a matter of direct communication and perhaps a reflection of the situation, whatever the situation may be at a given point in time. But in no way can this be applied as a rule, a general rule, and in no way can one always act in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we get to the relationship between the security organ at the brigade level and the military police, I want to show you what has come into evidence as P398. We could look at this. We have a copy for the ELMO. First of all, General, do you recall seeing this document at or around the time when it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's 389, by our view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. What did I say? Oh, okay, it's 389.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, General, do you recall seeing this document when it was generated? And from the date, you see 11 November 1994. 11 November 1994. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the 24th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Not at all, not back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, before coming to court today, have you had a chance to look at it, at this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to examine it somewhat?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And to the best of your ability, could -- in light of your position, background, experience, knowledge in the field, could you tell us whether this instruction in general or in principle follows the regulations and the laws with respect to the security or security and intelligence organ.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us -- you told us earlier about the one-third, two-thirds distinction, administrative versus counter-intelligence. Here we have this percentage of what would appear to be 80 and 20 per cent. Do you know where these numbers were plucked out of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure. I can't answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the one-third that you were referring to, would that be, with respect to what is being identified here as the tasks under 20 per cent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it the 80 per cent would be the 66 per cent -- or the two-thirds that you've indicated earlier?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention, if I could, on paragraph 3, under "Instructions," and in particular, I would like you to look at the -- and this would be on page 2 in the English version, Mr. Usher. And it's on the second page at the top of the page for both. I'm looking at the second paragraph of paragraph number 3, and it states here: "At the same time, to the extent and in the measure necessary, members of the security and intelligence organs must provide their immediate superiors with information, assessments and observations regarding the security of units or institutions." And what I want to focus your attention on is that particular language, where it says: "...to the extent and in the measure necessary," that portion. Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you please give us an explanation what exactly does that mean? And I believe you already told us a little bit, but I just want to hear your concrete observations.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said - I do not wish to repeat myself - the extent and measure necessary, this is not easily quantifiable and not easy to determine; however, the lower-level security organ is usually given a definition of this by the superior security organ commander. Rather, it is up to the security organ to assess what the extent and the measure should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At the brigade level, would that be the -- the head of the security organ? In other words, to the extent and the measure he thought necessary, he would inform his commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes. But most often if he was told to do so by the corps security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in looking at this -- that portion that we focussed on, it would appear that it's subject to some interpretation as to the latitude, the breadth.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you see any problems that that -- or any potential problems giving someone at the brigade level, for instance, a security officer, with this sort of latitude or discretionary power, if we want to put it that way, with respect to what and at which time and how much he would inform his commander on matters that would fit in with this -- in this 80 per cent or 66 percentile of counter-intelligence activity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This can produce an effect with security organs, especially in situations where the security organ is not sufficiently trained and is not sufficiently familiar with the laws and provisions, the laws and the rules. This can produce or lead to certain deviations or aberrations on this issue, and this cuts both ways. It can be that he totally keeps all information back from the commander or that he entirely neglects the basic fundamental principles of counter-intelligence work and shares all information at the very outset with the commander -- rather, informs the commander about everything. This can be a source of certain forms of negative behaviours, first and foremost by insufficiently trained security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I believe that's all I have for this document. Now, if we could focus our attention a little bit on the aspects of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I could have the kindness of Mr. Usher to bring it down a little bit. And before I go into this area too much, Mr. President, will we be breaking at our normal time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm not sure when will be the normal time. But if you feel, you know, time for a break, we will break at 12.00, or you just finished a section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would -- I would appreciate around 12.00, in light of my -- the situation on the ground here, my own physical strength today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to just briefly discuss with you this relationship between the security organ and the military police. Could you please tell us, at the brigade level now, first of all, who commands or who is in charge of the military police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The brigade commander exercises command and control over the military police, as over all other subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's his asset?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we know that a -- the military police have a commander -- a "komandir" of their own, but who is the commander of the military police, who is their immediate commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To what extent does the security organ get involved with the military police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: As I've pointed out, the security organ attached to the brigade, as for the work of the command in terms of planning and decision-making is concerned, it makes proposals for the deployment of military police units and presents this proposal to the brigade commander. At the same time, the security organ also has a role to play, in terms of professional guidance, in relation to military police services; namely, the services that we enumerated back at the outset. In practical terms, this means that any deployment or use of military police units is ordered and commanded by the commander of that unit. As for specific tasks, throughout the military police services the security organ has the authority to issue a task, an assignment to a section, department, or whatever the military police has, so that these tasks are then carried out by these individual services regardless of the commander, but they could and should inform the commander about the results of those activities, depending on the case or mission at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Can the chief of intelligence and security issue orders to the military police as he sees fit? In other words, however he feels at the time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Command is single. That applies to military police units. As to all other units, there is only one commander who exercises command over these units. In the case of brigade, this is the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about the superior security organs? Say, the -- the corps security organ, Popovic in this particular case? Can he under the rules, assuming we follow them, can he reach down and give direct orders to members of the military police of a brigade, such as the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what about Beara? He's at the Main Staff. He's --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe -- I believe I just finished that section, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll have a break and we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karnavas, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: General, I want to switch to some -- switch topics and get more focussed into the period that we are concerned with. And to start with, I would like to show you a document that has been introduced as P543. And if you could just look at it quickly, and then I'll -- I'll direct your attention to the appropriate segment. Now, sir, do you know what this document is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The heading shows that this is an order of the commander of the Drina Corps for active activities -- or rather, for the operation named Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe if we go all the way to the last page we see the author of this document, or the person who is -- takes responsibility for the contents of it. We see Major General Zivanovic. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you knew Mr. Zivanovic at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I knew him, but most probably he didn't know me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And it shows that he was the commander of the Drina Corps at that particular time. Now, if I could focus your attention, sir, I'd like to focus your attention to paragraph number 10. It would be on page -- page 6 in the English, page 4 in your version, with the title "Combat security." Look at that. Have you located it, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is security for combat activity. That's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, prior to coming here today, you -- I've shown you this document, have I not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, in fact, I've asked you to look at this particular paragraph, paragraph number 10, and specifically to go to the latter part of the paragraph that deals with the security organ in dealing with prisoners of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in looking at this paragraph or this section of the -- the order by General Zivanovic, could you please give us your interpretation or your expert analysis on this particular segment; that is, the dealing of -- with prisoners of war by the security organ.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The second part reads as follows: "In dealing with prisoners of war and the civilian population behave in every way in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." That's fine. However: "Security organs and military police will indicate the areas for gathering and securing prisoners of war and war booty," which precedes the other paragraph I read, this is incorrect and the corps commander did not specify this task properly. This is improper. The rules regulate this in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us how the rules regulate this aspect.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In the process of decision-making, when war prisoners and war booty are anticipated, the assistant commander for logistics makes a proposal and the corps commander adopts this proposal related to the localities where prisoners of war will be gathered and separately the localities where war booty will be collected. The operations organ in the staff proposes the way in which these localities will be secured. If the unit concerned has a military police unit, then the security organ proposes that the military police unit should secure the locations where war prisoners and war booty will be collected. Then all of that is translated into an order of this kind, and then the military police unit is given a task, or if there is no military police unit, then another unit is given the task specifically by the commander to provide security for prisoners of war -- or rather, the locality where prisoners of war will be gathered. In the order addressed to logistics and the rear services - and that is an integral part of the commander's order - that is where the place or locality where the war prisoners will be gathered and where war booty will be collected respectively. That is the way it should be in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let me -- let me touch on a couple of aspects of this answer. First of all, why is it necessary to have the rear services or the logistics sector or organ involved in this process?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, logistics or the rear services have many obligations regarding prisoners of war and war booty too. As regards prisoners of war, the location where they will be gathered, according to rules of combat, is usually in a different part of the area of that unit, where their in-depth positions are, because prisoners of war have to be fed; they have to receive proper medical care. Then perhaps their transport has to be organised from the actual collection point, and everything else. That means that they should have all the prescribed logistics support, and they should be accorded the treatment guaranteed by conventions dealing with the treatment of prisoners of war. That is why this locality has to be established in such a way that it is easily or readily accessible, so that the logistics or rear services can carry out their tasks properly. That is one of the reasons. Another one of the reasons is that such a place should not be close to the front end or the first line because of the possible dangers that could follow. That is the way it is regulated by the rules, and that is the way it should be regulated as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, aside from what you just told us, in looking at the way this is written, do you see any potential problems with giving the security organ these tasks in the manner in which -- that are outlined in this particular order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I think -- well, actually, in this way, security organs are charged with particular duties and tasks. They could take part in the security activities of the military police and also in the treatment of prisoners of war afterwards; that is to say, when they are interviewed and so on. This goes beyond the possibilities and level of training of these organs, in terms of producing results that would show that the task is not carried out completely or was carried out in part only. Then there can be other problems in this regard. Quite simply, security organs are not trained for dealing with all the measures that have to be taken in terms of this activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I believe that's all we have at this point in time with this document. Now, I want to share with you another document that has come in as P406, Exhibit P406. And to save a little time, I believe that you've -- I've shown you this document as well. It's dated July 5, 1995. And it's Colonel Blagojevic's order for active combat operations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, I asked you to look at the particular segment in Colonel Blagojevic's order with respect to prisoners of war, which would be -- I believe it's on page 5 of your -- of your document. It's also page 5 in the English document. It's under paragraph 10. Do you see that, sir, where it --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it says here that: "Prisoners of war and war booty will be collected in Pribicevac -- in the sector," and it's underlined: "Comply the Geneva Conventions in the treatment of prisoners of war and the population." My first question is: Sir, are you familiar with or acquainted with the -- with the Pribicevac sector?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Secondly, in reading this and in comparing it to what was ordered or in the order in which -- the manner which it was drafted in the order by General Zivanovic, can you please give us your expert opinion as to the manner in which Colonel Blagojevic has drafted his order.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The order of Colonel Blagojevic -- or rather, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade -- or rather, this particular position that we are commenting upon is correct in both cases; namely, the commander adopted somebody's proposal or decided independently when establishing an area, an area where prisoners of war and war booty are to be collected has to be established in the order. So from that point of view, this order is correct, and it reflects the way the rules regulate this subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you went to paragraph 12, which would be the last page - it would be page 7 - it says here that: "The IKM," the forward command post of the brigade, "would be in the Pribicevac sector." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you still maintain your position, the one that you've just stated, that Colonel Blagojevic's designation, specific designation of where the prisoners would be located, if and when any would be caught?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Since this has to do with the forward command post and that it is the area of Pribicevac, I'm not familiar with the area, but what has to be taken into account is the proximity of the first line -- or rather, the area where combat activities take place. I stand by what I said, that this is closer to the other end, that it is further away from the first line. It is closer to the rear command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you that at that location that would be where the commander would also be located during the critical period, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, that is, would that in any way affect your -- the opinion that you've already stated in either a positive or a negative fashion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I could not give any comments as to the reasons why the location was established in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention on -- on paragraph 5.6, and this would be on page 4, at the top of page 4, and it would be page 3, sir, General, it would be page 3 for you. 5.6, it says here: "The reserve: If necessary, have the Military Police Platoon ready for deployment in the sector of the Command Post of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade." Now, I have a pretty general question for you: Is this proper to have the Military Police Platoon as the reserve, or is this an abuse of that particular asset, a violation of the rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. This is an order for active combat activities and the unit was used in the right way -- or rather, it was given the right kind of task. In combat activities, only in exceptional cases, and in a situation of initial grouping, an effort is made always for this kind of reserve, and this was done quite correctly from the point of view of the rules that regulate the use of military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, before I go on to the next segment - and that would be the activities that took place after the fall of Srebrenica - could you please tell us where you were during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I believe that's -- you can -- that would be enough. And I'm through with this document as well.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Until the 15th of July, the evening of the 15th of July, I was in the area of responsibility of the 1st Infantry Brigade Novi Grad of the 1st Krajina Corps -- or the 2nd Krajina Corps, since in a certain period of time the brigade went from one corps to the other. But at any rate, it was the 1st Infantry Brigade Novi Grad. And on the 16th of July, I came to Han Pijesak -- or rather, to Crna Rijeka, the command post of the Main Staff, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how long you had been gone from the area. You told us you arrived back on the evening of the 15th of July. What was the period of your absence from this area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Without any interruption from the 5th of July -- or rather, the 4th of July, when I was given the task in relation to the 1st Brigade Novi Grad. Before that, I came every now and then from the 19th of March that year, and for the most part I was in the area of responsibility of the 1st or 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us what exactly you were doing from the 4th to the evening of the 15th of July. What were you engaged in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was on the team of the Main Staff that was viewing the causes and consequences of the loss of positions by this brigade where major losses were sustained, in terms of manpower and materiel at part of the positions of this brigade. That was the task, and that is what was being done. The deadline for carrying out this task was the 15th of July. That was the set deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you during that critical period, the ones that you've outlined, from the 4th until the -- the 15th, the evening of the 15th, did you in any way participate in any activities dealing with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Prior, prior to leaving for this particular task, that is, prior to July 4th, were you in any way consulted or did you in any way get involved in the activities regarding the -- the events surrounding Srebrenica, that were to follow, that is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During that period, were you ever contacted by Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your -- during that -- that period while you were absent, were you getting any reports or any information with respect to what had happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During that period of time, were you engaged with in any way, with the military police, with respect to any activities that would be connected or linked to Srebrenica and the events that followed afterwards?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, during that period of time - and let me just focus your attention on two critical days, the 12th and the 13th of July, 1995 - did you ever visit Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or were you in the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the area that you were in, what would be the distance? How far away would you be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The road one usually takes, it would be between 450 and 500 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, since you weren't there on those days, the 12th, the 13th and onwards, perhaps I can give you some -- some information with respect to Potocari and maybe you can help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, providing a witness information is -- it would be leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's why I phrased it that way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what kind of information. This witness testified that he was not even there during that period. I don't know the purpose for you to provide those information to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- I phrased it in such a way that at least I would be alarming everybody of what I was about to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are alarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was -- well, let me put it this way, Your Honour: In light of the gentleman's position, even though he was absent, I was going to pose a series of questions with respect to who would be responsible for the individuals in Potocari and then the prisoners that were separated, keeping in mind that he wasn't there. Now, in order for me to do that, I would have to give him some -- some of the facts that have already come in. Now, if I'm not permitted because the Court may decide that the gentleman, since he wasn't there and has no firsthand knowledge would not be competent at least to discuss that, I -- I will accept that, but I certainly don't want those questions being asked on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it depends, you know. Sometimes the hearsay evidence is also admissible, so you may try. But -- but I'm not sure about, you know, the results. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it sounds like Mr. Karnavas is using this person as perhaps an expert witness on the very fundamental issues of the case. First of all, we haven't had any notice of anything like that, and it's perfectly appropriate for him to talk about the rules, as he has done, and how they are applied, and we can all take our knowledge of this case and apply them, but to take him to some place where he says he knows nothing about and was not there at this stage really is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may briefly respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The gentleman, years ago - I'm using the plural - was questioned by the OTP, so they certainly knew this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we're going to get into that, I think we need to -- we need to start having discussions outside the presence of the -- the witness. I just don't know what comes next when we start getting into the history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I was merely responding because they said they had no notice. The gentleman lives in Banja Luka. They questioned him. They talked to him about those events. So certainly -- it's not as if, you know, I've just introduced somebody that they had absolutely no knowledge of. And they've questioned the gentleman. Now, if I'm forbidden into that area, I can accept that decision, so long as the Prosecution is forbidden from venturing into those areas. That's all. I just want to know what the rules of engagement are. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You are being, as I'm sure you understand, being put in a position where Mr. Karnavas is trying to make deals with the Court, which -- that he wants to get a pre-emptive ruling against what I can go into on cross-examination. That's absurd and improper and is -- should be out of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we allowed you to go into this area, but bear in mind that this witness was absent during that time and all we heard will be the hearsay evidence. We will see how far you could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll just ask some foundational questions and take it from there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: General, I know you weren't there, but since that period, did you -- have you had a chance to learn about meetings that were held between General Mladic and the DutchBat and representatives of the Muslim community there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My next question: Do you feel sufficiently knowledgeable or confident in being able to discuss as to who would be responsible for the individuals that had left Srebrenica and had gathered to Potocari, some of whom were evacuated, some of whom were separated and eventually killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I know, I can't say who was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just one question. I think you -- since you -- and you might be able to assist us here. Would Nikolic in that critical -- those critical days, would he have been in a position to directly order the military police to go and perform various tasks in Potocari without first seeking the approval of the commander, that is, Commander Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Would he have been in a position? I don't know. But if he had done that, that would not have been a correct thing to do, not a proper thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I believe you told us earlier, but just in case I wasn't -- I'm not clear on this. Would he have been able to conduct activities with Popovic and Beara on his own without consulting or getting the approval of his commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's rather vague "would he have been able."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would he have been able. But if your question is according to the rules, that's perfectly non-objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I did qualify it, but I'll rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During these critical days when all sorts of activity went on, was Momir Nikolic free to go about and carry on or carry out tasks and orders issued to him by Popovic and Beara without first notifying his commander and perhaps even getting the approval of his commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: To bring in the concept of free and freedom, that really throws a monkey-wrench into the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps the gentleman could -- if he understood my question, perhaps he can answer it. If freedom is such a very difficult concept, something that we hear every day from -- you know, on TV, especially these days, coming out of Iraq, I think the gentleman can -- can certainly answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think without that word "free," the sentence still stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. Based on the existing laws and regulations governing service in the military, he would not have been allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I just want to show you one document. It has been introduced already. It's P687. It's a document that was generated by President Karadzic addressed to Miroslav Deronjic, president of the SDS, who was appointed the commissioner. And I want you to look at it, and particularly if you could pay close attention to paragraphs number 4 and 5. Okay. Now -- and again, if you feel sufficiently confident and competent to answer this question, in light of your position and background, even though this is a document to a civilian organ, in reading paragraphs 4 and 5, do you have an opinion as to what Deronjic's responsibility would have been or should have been or were in fact, based on what President Karadzic's decision [sic]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This document speaks for itself. I don't see how this witness is in any position to be commenting on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And as you pointed out, Mr. Karnavas, this is for the civilian branches, not for the military ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I qualified it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand. So we don't know the purpose, you know, for you to ask this question to this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I just -- very well, Your Honour. But I take it since Mr. McCloskey said the document speaks for itself, it's speaking to me that Deronjic was in charge. Would that -- is that what Mr. McCloskey meant by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we could read the document by ourselves. As for what kind of conclusion we draw, it's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I -- I take it I should move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I think this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I think this document -- we shouldn't have any problem, General. It's Exhibit P500, a document given to us by the Office of the Prosecution. Have you seen this document before, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what does this document refer to, at least with respect to you specifically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This document refers to the fact that at one point in time, specifically on the 17th of July, the commander of the Main Staff ordered that part of the Krivaja 95 operation, or rather, the completion of the search of the terrain along the line of movement of the 28th Division from Srebrenica, I should be the one to take over command over all units within the area -- or rather, the units enumerated in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's talk about those events. First of all, were you ever given an order? And if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I never received personally this written document, but I did receive the order in this form at the command post in the Main Staff from the commander of the Main Staff. As for who wrote the document, that was done by the chief of the operations organ in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, specifically, what were the orders given to you as you understood them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The task given to me by General Mladic was roughly as described in this document. I'm not sure if this is a totally accurate interpretation, but essentially it is accurate, yes. Myself, I don't know about this other thing concerning involvement at stage 2 between Drinjaca and Cerska. This is something I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please continue, General. Okay. Let me go on to my next question. Now, in this particular task, were you going as part of the security organ or in some other capacity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. And as --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What's the objection about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How -- in what capacity are you going? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it could have been going in a variety of capacities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is the proper way to ask the question, and I just -- to try to help prevent me having to jump up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is the direct examination, Mr. Karnavas. You should not put a leading question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, if I was suggesting information. Now, as I indicated, OTP questioned the man, and we had lots of testimony that he's from the security organ, so that wasn't leading. I wasn't suggesting. And I said if he was going in another -- in another capacity. I didn't give a suggestion as to what other capacities he might have been going, so I don't see the problem, but I'll ask -- I'll rephrase, Your Honour. I'm rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yeah. Rephrase your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In what capacity were you going?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- or rather, I can't say in what capacity I was going. What I can say is that, as I said at the outset, I was working with the security administration of the military police of the Main Staff, if what's what you mean by "capacity." This specific task that is set out in this document is redefined and modified. If I had pursued this task, I would have gone there as the commander of units, as stated in the document, but it was not in the -- the capacity of commander that I went, because in the evening hours the task had been modified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please explain how it had been modified.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This task is unrealistic, and that was my assessment at the time, and I let the commander of the Main Staff know how I felt about it and that I was not able to carry it out, like this. I did this in the presence of two of his assistants. He did not accept this. He walked out of the room in which we were talking. The role of mediator to have this decision modified was taken up by General Tolimir. He followed the commander out, and in his own room, in front of the building itself, he stayed with him for several hours. It was late in the evening that he told me that I would still go and tour this area, that I would not take over command over those units. He said that I would talk to the superior officers of the units under the blockade and that we would search the terrain and that then I would be able to assess how the operation was going and I would report back to him on that. So that was the redefined task. Now, in which capacity I was there exactly, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you -- thank you, General. Now, did you go to the -- did you go to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall what day it was that you went to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I have not memorised the date. I know that it was one day, based on some documents, this particular document also, and other similar documents from other units. I narrowed the time span down to two possible days, the 17th or the 18th, but I can't say which of the two it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you went to Bratunac, did you meet with anyone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With whom did you meet?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: At the command of the Bratunac Brigade, I looked for the brigade commander in the morning hours, give or take an hour or two, I'm not sure, but I located him. I found him at the command post, and that was also where we met, because we had not known each other previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what happened when you met the commander of the Bratunac Brigade at the command post of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: He told me that activities on that day were unfolding the same way as the previous day, in relation to searching the terrain. He said that some units had been blocked and that some of the military units, the army's units and the MUP units, a small fraction of those, were searching the ground along the Bratunac-Milici-Konjevic Polje road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And based on that information, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Following my return to the Main Staff, I passed on the information and said that those activities were well underway and that probably they would be completed by the end of that day or perhaps the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did Colonel Blagojevic at any point in time describe to you the relationship between MUP and the VRS troops?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you on that particular day go to the field to give any orders or to make an inspection as to how the activities were being carried out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In part I did carry out an inspection. But as for going to the field and visiting the units who were searching the ground, no, I did not go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how and to what extent you carried out this inspection.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: By talking to the units, starting with the first unit, which was a military police company belonging to the military police battalion of the Protection Motorised Regiment, between Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje, I spoke to the battalion commander, Major Malinic. Further down to Konjevic Polje, I met one of the officers from the communications regiment, whose identity, or rather, name I can't remember. Finally, in Konjevic Polje itself, I learned -- I didn't talk to anyone in particular. I learned that the Engineers Unit of the Drina Corps, and then further down from Konjevic Polje, outside Bratunac or I can't say where precisely there were some forces of the Bratunac Brigade at -- along that road. That was as much as I was able to see, especially the blockade along the route where it was supposed to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you carry out any inspection with MUP units, assuming that that was part of your portfolio?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. I found out then that some of their units were on the ground. I didn't see them, but in Bratunac I met who I believed was the Chief of Staff of the Special MUP Brigade, Mr. Borovcanin, and another officer from the same units, whose name I really can't remember. This MUP officer, I saw him somewhere along the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje. I never had any other contact with MUP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on that day, did you learn whether any prisoners had been taken or captured?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The only thing I did learn about prisoners on that day was in relation to Major Malinic, who in our conversation told me that on the football pitch in Nova Kasaba between two and 3.000 people had been assembled, between two and 3.000 prisoners, and that they had been taken to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had Major Malinic told you who had issued those orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The order for the prisoners to be taken from the football pitch in Kasaba to Bratunac had been issued to him personally by the commander of the Main Staff when he was passing by the football pitch, and he personally addressed those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever learn what happened to those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what you learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection as to foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could have an idea when he learned this, it would make more sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I think I can do my direct in the fashion in which I wish to, because the following question is when -- I don't need to ask it in the order in which the Prosecutor is directing me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, just so far as -- to have a better understanding of the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe -- maybe if the time frame, you know, comes first would be much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it might -- okay, very well, Your Honour. If I'm being given instruction by the Court, not a problem. But, you know, usually what, when, how, we get to those eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the Prosecutor's sake, could you please tell us when you learned what happened to the men.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: As for the fact that something had happened or that a crime had occurred, there were rumours just after the war. The first direct personal knowledge that I had about this was from the trial of the Sabotage Detachment, when Erdemovic and Kremenovic were tried before this Court. As for more comprehensive information on all these events, that was over the last year, following a decision of the human rights council in relation to the events surrounding Srebrenica and an investigation undertaken by Republika Srpska in relation to those events, and this is the first time that these matters have been discussed openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you at any point in time conduct your own investigation, a separate one? And I'm not asking you about what the RS is doing but one within the security organ.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid I do not understand your question. But specifically I do not know of any investigation being conducted by the security organs in relation to the events that took place in and around Srebrenica or that they did that independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did Colonel Beara ever tell you what he had been involved with during those days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about Popovic? I believe he was a lieutenant colonel with the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a lieutenant colonel in the Drina Corps, and he never talked to me specifically about what happened or the circumstances concerning his engagement at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, staying with the -- with the day that you went to Bratunac to carry out these activities, whether it was the 17th or the 18th, to your recollection, could you please tell us what else you did on that day, if anything.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, on that day, in addition to this, I had a few other engagements. One of them was to find Colonel Jankovic from the intelligence administration of the Main Staff, which was done, since when asked to do so, he did come to the command post of the Bratunac Brigade shortly after my arrival. I was supposed to tell him of a few engagements that he was supposed to carry out. One was to return arms and equipment that the units of the Army of Republika Srpska took from the UNPROFOR troops - that is to say, the Dutch Battalion - at checkpoints. The other task he had was to go to the command of the Dutch Battalion in order to convey information -- or rather, reach agreement on the evacuation, because in the meantime it was decided that the evacuation of the Dutch Battalion would take place across the Drina River -- that is to say, via Serbia -- or rather, via the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, not via Sarajevo or Sarajevo airport. Jankovic and I were also supposed to find someone from the Ministry of the Interior in order to convey to them that the evacuation of the Dutch Battalion would be the responsibility of the Ministry of the Interior and of Mr. Tomo Kovac personally. Those were my activities in that day -- on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, where did you go after that? Where did you spend the night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I think it was at the command post at Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you at any point in time go to Zvornik, to the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Han Pijesak is in the opposite direction, once you get to the intersection of Konjevic Polje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that you were somewhat unclear about -- as to the date. I want to show you Exhibit P265. Could you please look at this. Perhaps this may assist in some way. It's a document given to us by the Prosecutor, an intercept. The date we have been told is the 17th, and it has "1115 hours," so that would be 11.15 in the morning. Could you please look at that. First of all, do you see your name on this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that I'm mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you just please look at it and tell us whether this intercept would have any relation to your visit to the Bratunac Brigade pursuant to the order that you had been issued by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The message shows that I was being sought. I cannot see from the message where I was at that moment, but I do not preclude the possibility of being on that day, the 17th, on that road, precisely due to the fact that I'm not sure which date this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But assuming that this was the 17th, as we've been told, it says here -- there's a question: "Has Kremenovic set off?" And then it says: "Well, we met him when we were on our way here." "Well, he hasn't come to me yet." "Well, in that case, what will happen is that he first went ahead over there to Momir Nikolic." Now, from this, can you help us out here. First of all, we have here a time, 11.15. Your arrival at the Bratunac Brigade, would that have been at this -- at around this time, before, or after, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, in the morning -- it must have been in the morning, because in the early afternoon hours, again at the command post I was looking for Colonel Blagojevic. I don't know why, but I no longer managed to find him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what about Momir Nikolic? It says here something -- something about: "Well, in that case, what will happen is that he first went ahead over there to Momir Nikolic." Why would you go to visit a captain, who was not even a first class captain, a reservist, even though he's in the security organ, to a colonel at the time from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: There could have been reason for me to see Nikolic, but I did not -- or rather, I don't know. I did not know Momir Nikolic at all. Had it not been for this trial, I probably never would have got to know him. So why he was not at the command at that point in time and why he was not in Bratunac is something that I don't know. I cannot say at all, in relation to him, where he was and what he was doing, but I don't know -- I don't remember ever having been in contact with him in any way, not personally. So before Blagojevic or afterwards, I did not see Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One last question: Based on the order that you had received from General Mladic, with whom were you supposed to make contact with or to whom were you supposed to report once you arrived at the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to report to the commander of the brigade, Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid we won't be able to finish today. I have just a little bit left for tomorrow, and so I -- I think this is a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I'm afraid that you have to stay in The Hague for another day, and during your stay please remember that you are still under the oath, so do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. There's an announcement for the schedule for tomorrow, and tomorrow we'll sit in the Courtroom II for the whole day, and the morning session will start from 10.00 until 11.30, and we'll have a long break, about two hours and a half, and we'll resume at 2.00 until 5.30 in the afternoon, which means that each sitting will last 90 minutes. Well, the hearing for today is adjourned.
